title: “Washington Stole the Election from Me. It Happened in Honduras and It Can Happen in Mexico”
author: Alejandro Páez Varela and Álvaro Delgado Gómez
content:
_This article by[Alejandro Páez Varela and Álvaro Delgado
Gómez](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/paez-delgado/) originally appeared in
the [October 9, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4884690/washington-me-robo-la-eleccion-
paso-en-honduras-y-puede-pasar-en-mexico-entrevista/)._

_Rixi Moncada accused Donald Trump of intervening in the Honduran elections
and denounced a mafia operation to prevent the victory of the left._

**Mexico City, October 9 (SinEmbargo).–** **Washington** intervened to prevent
her victory in [**Honduras**](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4800346/complot-
continental-contra-la-izquierda-de-mexico-y-colombia-que-es-el-hondurasgate/),
turned the election into **" a great mafia operation"** and used everything
from the direct pressure of **Donald Trump** to disinformation networks and
international structures to impose a result, charged **Rixi Moncada** , former
presidential candidate of the **Liberty and Refoundation Party** (Libre).

The Honduran leader warned in an interview with **Alejandro Páez and Álvaro
Delgado** on the program "Los Periodistas," which is broadcast on the YouTube
channel of **SinEmbargo Al Aire** , that what happened in her country is not
an isolated case, but rather a laboratory of new forms of political
interference that can be repeated in Mexico: "Don't be overconfident," she
cautioned. "You are not exempt from this. It is going to happen and it must be
prevented."

Moncada, who officially finished in third place in the 2025 Honduran elections
with 19.19 percent of the votes, rejected those results and maintained that
they were the product of an operation prepared over months. She recalled that
three days before the election Trump publicly called for people not to vote
for her and backed **Nasry Asfura** , who was ultimately declared the winner;
in addition, two days before, the U.S. president announced the pardon of
former president Juan Orlando Hernández, convicted in the United States of
drug trafficking.

For Moncada, those actions, added to the audios of the so-called Honduras
Gate, show how "the right reformulated its form of attack" on democracies and
expanded its mechanisms of intervention through social networks,
disinformation campaigns, and international operatives.

In that sense, Moncada called for what happened in Honduras to be taken
seriously. She noted that the known evidence shows that interventions in
electoral processes can no longer be treated as mere suspicions and warned
that no country is exempt from facing manipulation strategies.

> "I believe that the first thing is that we must take the issue with total
> seriousness, starting from that reality that has been left, not like in
> other times when it remains as doubt; right now it is exposed, as I said
> before, with full proof."

The former candidate stressed that her call does not consist of abandoning the
democratic path or resorting to violence. On the contrary, she maintains that
the defense of political freedoms must be accompanied by an economic
transformation that reduces the concentration of wealth and limits the power
of financial groups.

"What to say to the Mexican people? That we do not propose alternatives that
are not democratic and peaceful. That our fundamental proposal, alongside the
political proposal of democracy and pacifism, the economic proposal must be
sustained," she stated.

In that sense, she recognized in Mexico an experience from which the Honduran
left can learn. She mentioned the denunciations that Andrés Manuel López
Obrador made for years about the fraudulent mechanisms of previous electoral
processes, as well as the continuity of the political project with the arrival
of Claudia Sheinbaum to the Presidency.

> "I believe that we, in the first place, have a lot to learn from Mexico and
> from the governments of López Obrador, from the struggle of Andrés Manuel
> from the left in the previous periods, the ones he denounced, the fraudulent
> forms now perfected. We have a lot to learn from that whole process, but
> then from how the Mexican people were able to sustain the great project in
> favor of themselves with Claudia. So, that experience nourishes us," she
> expressed.

Moncada considered that the Mexican experience demonstrates the importance of
peoples being able to sustain their political projects, but warns that this
continuity must not be taken for granted. Intervention strategies, she
maintained, change form and seek to adapt to the conditions of each country.

![Rixi Moncada talks with Álvaro Delgado in the SinEmbargo
studio](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/moncada-
washington-02-studio.jpg)Rixi Moncada, former presidential candidate of
Honduras, asserted that Washington's interference marked her country's
election and warned that this model can be repeated in Mexico. Photo: Crisanto
Rodríguez, SinEmbargo

## Moncada Points to Washington for Interference

Rixi Moncada asserted that what happened during the elections in Honduras was
not something improvised, but rather a strategy planned well in advance with
the objective of stealing the result.

> I believe that in Honduras a good laboratory of the right was set up well in
> advance, where that criminal network each carried out its phase in what I
> say, they were not elections, it was a great mafia operation to steal the
> elections; they put it into practice, it worked for them.
>
> Rixi Moncada

Moncada maintained that the U.S. intervention was neither an isolated event
nor an unfounded suspicion. She asserted that during the six months prior to
the election in Honduras an operation was prepared in which different actors
participated, and that the arrest of Fernando Cerimedo confirms the complaints
that her movement had filed with the Honduran Public Prosecutor's Office.

"The news reconfirms our hypothesis and reconfirms what had been happening
throughout the last six months of preparation of the electoral process, but
above all gives validity to the complaint that had already been made in
Honduras before the Public Prosecutor's Office about some audios that showed a
criminal network that was operating from within spaces of power inside
Honduras to steal the elections with international support," she stated.

![Fernando Cerimedo, Donald Trump Jr., Brad Parscale and Dick Morris
meeting](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/moncada-
washington-03-cerimedo-trump-jr.jpg)From left to right: Andy Rivas (back
turned), Fernando Cerimedo, Donald Trump Jr., Brad Parscale and Dick Morris.
Photo: Facebook Nadia Beller

For the former candidate, the events exposed a strategy that goes beyond
irregularities at the ballot box. It was, she asserted, about organizing
political operations with foreign intervention, manipulating information, and
using different mechanisms to prevent the will of the citizens from
translating into a change of government.

"I believe that for the audiences of the Latin American region, for the
audiences of the entire world, whoever had doubts about how a supposedly
democratic operation for an electoral process is put together, how it is
prepared or how it is organized, how in reality what it has behind it is a
great criminal network to hold on to power at all costs and to disguise our
democracies, from the perspective of all the actions of Fernando Cerimedo and
his interventions and his interference to the tune of the clear interference
of President Donald J. Trump, they are a total reality. There is no doubt
about that. There is, let's say, full proof of what is happening with our
liberal democracies on the continent," she maintains.

Moncada directly pointed to Trump for intervening in the days prior to the
vote. According to her account, the U.S. president asked Hondurans not to vote
for her three days before the election and, two days before, announced the
pardon of former president Juan Orlando Hernández, sentenced in the United
States to 45 years in prison for drug trafficking.

> "Trump's direct interference was three days before. Three days before he
> says: 'Don't vote for Rixi Moncada,' but then two days before the elections
> he says: 'There I send you the narco sentenced to 45 years, former president
> Juan Orlando Hernández,'" she explained.

The former candidate considered that those actions were part of a broader
operation, in which, she denounced, different resources were used to condition
the electoral process and favor the sectors of the right. Among the mechanisms
she described is the so-called "embarazo de urnas" (ballot box
"impregnating"), a practice that, she explained, makes it possible to annul
votes through claims of supposed alterations in certain polling stations.

"Impregnating ballot boxes, as we call it here, to annul them. So that the
polling stations don't pass, so that right there at the polling stations they
say: 'No, well, this one is altered.' So, the selected ballot boxes,
obviously, where the opposition can win, and that is a fraud, already a direct
participation of electoral organized crime," she denounced.

Based on that experience, Moncada proposed that the Latin American lefts must
prepare to confront operations that, from her perspective, seek to strip
peoples of their right to freely elect their rulers. It is not enough, she
said, to denounce fraud once it occurs, but rather to build a political and
social organization capable of responding to interference before the
mechanisms of intervention are set in motion.

> X](https://twitter.com/riximga/status/2091244952311210236)

## The Right Perfects Its Mechanisms

For the former candidate, one of the main changes in the strategies of the
right lies in the terrain of communication. She stated that her adversaries
maintain a discourse in favor of clean and transparent elections, while
resorting to mechanisms that, from her perspective, intervene in the
consciousness of citizens and condition their political decision.

> "The right reformulated its form of attack on democracy. They, too, are not
> willing to step outside and they say: 'There must be elections and the
> elections must be clean, transparent,' and they handle that in their
> discourse. So, how did they reformulate their attack? Here is an element
> that I consider important: they reformulated that form of attack by entering
> into the process of consciousness and exercise of freedom of the people
> through the empire of communications," she explained.

Moncada pointed to digital platforms as one of the spaces where that dispute
is fought. In her judgment, the spread of lies and falsehoods through social
networks makes it possible to influence the perception of citizens and weaken
their capacity to make decisions with truthful information.

"And so there, how is the domination? I believe they are exercising it through
what could be an addiction to telecommunications on the new platforms. They
are exercising domination via the lie, via falsehood, but through that
addiction to TikTok, to the networks," she maintained.

For that reason, she insisted that the defense of democracy requires a
permanent presence in the territories and direct work with the population.
From her perspective, political forces cannot limit themselves to competing
every four years at the ballot box, since they must also confront the
conditions that allow external actors and economic groups to intervene in
electoral processes.

> "It is time to organize territories, it is time to go to the territories and
> organize our people. No, it is not just an issue of elections, right? It is
> not an issue of a ballot box and a ballot paper and of submitting in four
> years to a new electoral process, because what for? To a new electoral
> process if it can have, if it is going to have interference, we already know
> it, if it is going to be fired upon from all sides until having the results
> that they themselves are proposing," she stated.

The former candidate noted that economic interests also take part in that
dispute for power. She considered in that sense that capital, the right, and
greed seek to impose their own results and prevent political projects that
question their privileges from reaching the government.

"And who proposes those results? Well, you know, and from the experiences of
Mexico too, capital proposes it, the right proposes it, ambition proposes it,
greed," she added.

From that perspective, Moncada maintained that the confrontation is not
limited to parties or candidates, but rather pits those who seek to preserve
the concentration of wealth against those who defend a social transformation.
For that reason, she affirmed that the left is not willing to give up the
historic conquests it attributes to the struggles of the peoples.

"We are not willing to hand over what we believe we have historically built
over the bodies, over the corpses, over the struggle of the peoples, over
misery and poverty; we are not willing to hand it over. And we don't care
whether democracy, whether principles, I mean, our scale of values is this.
And on this scale of values we are going to be owners of the governments and
we are going to be owners of the territories and of the people and of their
economies and of their resources, and the poor, let it go on, then," she
maintained.

And she summed up that dispute as a conflict between a minority that
concentrates power and the majority of the population: "One percent against 99
percent in the entire world. That's what it is, I mean, history, well,
repeating itself."

## The Response: Popular Organization

Faced with that scenario, Moncada mentioned that the Latin American lefts must
build a joint response. The Honduran experience, she said, forces them to
think about how to combat foreign interference, confront manipulation
operations, and communicate to citizens what, from her perspective, is
happening in their countries.

> "I receive it accepting the reality of our countries, but with the internal
> strength for how we combat interference, how we combat meddling, how we
> reach the consciousness of our peoples, how we communicate to our peoples
> that they are today being governed by these presidents who have turned their
> backs on our own peoples and who are in favor of the oligarchies," she said.

The former candidate recognized President Claudia Sheinbaum and the Mexican
people as important references for the Honduran left, but warned that the
defense of a political project cannot depend solely on who occupies the
Presidency. Social organization must be maintained even when progressive
forces do not control the government.

"Now we only have Mexico left, with affection, fondness, recognition for
Claudia, right?, and for the Mexican people, who have other historical
connotations, but then, how do we get that message across? I believe that is
the challenge," she noted.

For Moncada, the task is to bring together the popular movements and the
forces of the left in the region to defend sovereignty and the freedom of
peoples to elect their rulers without interference. The work, she insists,
must continue from the spaces of organization that each movement preserves,
without waiting for a new electoral process to arrive.

"Uniting among the lefts, uniting the peoples, organizing the peoples from our
spaces of power. We don't have the government, but from our spaces of popular
power, organizing ourselves, uniting, and continuing to build the project of
life in which we believe," she concluded.
